notes.meaning: The 'great cloud of witnesses' is the huge crowd of faithful people from chapter 11. They are witnesses because their lives show that God keeps His promises. The picture is a race. Runners throw off anything heavy, so we should drop whatever slows us down, especially the sin that wraps around our feet. Then we keep running and don't quit.

differ.view: Some believe the saints in heaven really do watch our race, like a crowd in the stands cheering us on.
Many say the saints are 'witnesses' because they gave testimony to God's faithfulness. They do not take it to mean the saints are watching us now.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some popular teaching blames our besetting sins (the sins we fall into most easily) on demons. Others answer that this verse simply calls us to lay sin aside in the Spirit's power.

notes.meaning: Look away from everything else and fix your eyes on Jesus. He is the one who starts our faith and carries it through to the end. He endured the pain and shame of the cross because He looked past it to the joy beyond it. Now He sits at God's right hand, the place of highest honor and power.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern translations say 'pioneer and perfecter.' This pictures Jesus as the one who went first and showed faith fully. They also hear an echo of Psalm 110:1.

notes.meaning: Think hard about Jesus and compare His suffering with yours. He faced constant opposition and hatred from sinners, and He never gave up. If the Lord bore all this, His servants can bear their share. Remembering Him keeps us from getting worn out and losing heart before the finish line.

The readers had lost property and been insulted for their faith. But none of them had yet been killed for it. In their fight against sin, including the pull to give up their faith, they had not yet faced the hardest test. So they should not quit now.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some teach 'let go and let God,' as if any effort of our own is wrong. Others point to this verse as a call for believers to actively resist and strive against sin.

notes.meaning: The writer quotes Proverbs 3:11-12, where God speaks to us as a loving father speaks to his children. There are two wrong ways to handle hard times. One is to shrug them off. The other is to collapse in despair. God's discipline means His training and correction, and it is proof of His love, not a sign that He has rejected us.
Accept hard times as God's training. When He corrects you, He is treating you as His own children. Every good father corrects his son. So we should expect our Father in heaven to do the same.

All of God's true children share in His discipline, some more and some less. A father who doesn't care about a child he refuses to own never bothers to train him. So someone who is left to go on in sin with no correction at all has reason to worry. It may show that he is not truly God's child.
Our earthly fathers corrected us, and we still respected them. God is the Father of our spirits, so we should submit to Him even more. The result is real life, both now and forever.

Earthly parents trained us for a short time, doing what seemed best to them. Sometimes they were too strict and sometimes too soft. God never gets it wrong. He always disciplines us for our good, so that we can share in His holiness, which means becoming pure and good like Him.
No discipline feels nice at the time. It hurts. But like an athlete's hard training, it pays off later. It grows a harvest of right living and inner peace in people who let it train them.

These words come from Isaiah 35:3 and Proverbs 4:26. Lift your tired arms and steady your shaky knees, and take courage again. Keep to a straight, level path so that weaker believers who limp along don't get knocked off course but get healed. This is about helping one another as well as yourself.

Work hard at living in peace with everyone, even with people who cause you trouble. Work just as hard at holiness, which means being set apart for God and living a pure life. Peace with people must never mean giving up holiness. Without holiness no one will see the Lord, that is, enjoy being with Him.

differ.view: Believers should press on toward complete holiness of heart and life. Not pursuing all holiness is the direct road into every kind of sin.
We must strive for holiness. Yet Christ Himself is the holiness without which no one sees God, and we see God only with eyes He has renewed.

notes.meaning: Watch over one another so that no one lags behind and misses out on God's grace, His free kindness to us. A 'root of bitterness' comes from Deuteronomy 29:18. It is a person, or a wrong teaching or way of life, that grows up and poisons many. It must be dealt with before it spreads.

differ.view: It is easy to fall away, so we must stay watchful. But the care that keeps us faithful is itself God's gift.
The grace God plants in a true believer's heart never fails. Here 'grace' means the gospel message of grace.
The verse warns that a person may 'fall from the grace of God.'
Some hold that this verse shows a person can truly fall away from grace they once had.

notes.meaning: Don't let anyone be sexually immoral or godless like Esau. Being godless here means treating holy things as cheap. Esau traded his birthright, the special rights of the oldest son, for a single meal. Those rights included a place in the family line of God's promises. The warning is not to trade our place with God for comfort or an easier life.

Later Esau wanted the blessing and begged for it with tears, but he was turned away. Many say he could not change his father Isaac's mind. Others say there was simply no way to undo what he had done. Either way, his tears were about his loss, not sorrow for his sin, since he went on to plan his brother's murder. The verse does not teach that someone who truly wants to turn back to God will be refused.

You have not come to Mount Sinai, the real, physical mountain where God gave the Law. It had fire, darkness, storm and a loud trumpet. When God's own voice spoke, the people were so afraid that they begged Him to stop. They asked to hear Him through Moses instead.

The people could not bear the strict command that even an animal touching the mountain must be put to death. The sight was so frightening that even Moses, God's friend, trembled. Exodus does not record these exact words of Moses, though Deuteronomy 9:19 has similar ones. All this showed God's awesome holiness under the old covenant, God's agreement with Israel through Moses.

Instead, believers have come to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, the city where the living God lives. 'You have come' means this is already true by faith. We are already citizens there, not just hoping to be one day. We join countless angels gathered in joyful celebration.

We also join the church of the firstborn. This is all of God's people, each given the honor of an oldest child, with names written in heaven like a list of citizens. We come before God, who is the Judge of everyone. We are joined with the spirits of righteous people who have died and now live with God, made perfect and free from sin.

Best of all, we come to Jesus, the mediator, or go-between, who brings God and people together in the new covenant. We come to His blood, shed for us and 'sprinkled' to make us clean, like the blood in the old sacrifices. Abel's blood cried out to God for justice against his murderer, but Jesus' blood pleads for mercy. Some older writers take Abel's 'blood' to mean his sacrifice, which Christ's sacrifice far surpasses.

So don't turn away from God, who speaks to us through Christ in the gospel. At Sinai God gave His warning on earth, and the people who refused it did not escape. He now speaks to us from heaven. If we turn away from Him, we have even less hope of escape.

At Sinai God's voice shook the earth. In Haggai 2:6 He promised to shake heaven and earth 'once more,' one last time. Everything created that can be shaken will be removed, and only what cannot be shaken will remain. Many say this shaking began when Christ first came and the old system of temple sacrifices passed away. They say it will be completed when He comes again.

We are receiving a kingdom that can never be shaken or replaced. So let us be thankful and worship God in a way that pleases Him, with deep respect and awe. Older translations say 'let us have grace.' That means holding on to the grace God gives us, which makes this kind of worship possible.

This line is quoted from Deuteronomy 4:24. The God of the gospel is the same holy God who spoke at Sinai. He is perfectly pure and just, and like fire He burns away sin. This is a serious warning to anyone who turns their back on Him.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some popular teachers take the fire mainly as God's testing. They say it clears the way for the Holy Spirit to change us and set us on fire for Him.
